cues.text: Let's turn now to a pair of ideas that students very often blur together: iterative development and incremental development.
They sound alike, and they frequently happen side by side, but they answer two different questions.
Start with iterative development.
Iterative development revises, or refines, a solution through repeated cycles.
The key word is repeated.
You do not try to get a feature perfect in one pass.
You build a version, look at how it performs, and improve it, then go round again.
The example given is improving search accuracy with each iteration.
The first cycle produces a search that works somewhat.
The next cycle makes it more accurate.
The cycle after that refines it further.
The same piece of the product is being revisited and made better.
Now incremental development.
Incremental development adds usable portions of capability.
Here the question is not "how do we make this better?" but "what new piece can we add?" The examples given are tracking, notifications, and billing.
Each of those is a distinct portion of capability.
You deliver tracking, and users can use it.
Later you add notifications.
Later still, billing.
The product grows by adding pieces.
So, to hold the distinction clearly: iterative is about revising and refining through repeated cycles; incremental is about adding usable portions of capability.
The source also tells us that they often coexist.
In a sprint, for example, a team adds new capability, which is the incremental part, and also refines existing features, which is the iterative part.
Both are happening in the same sprint.
Let us look at the incremental process step by step, in order.
First, identify and prioritise requirements.
Second, partition them into coherent increments, and work out the dependencies between them.
Third, design, develop, and test each increment.
Fourth, integrate and deliver.
Fifth, gather feedback.
Sixth, improve and plan the next increment.
Notice that the sixth step leads back into planning, so the process continues as a loop of growth.
The iterative phases run like this.
Plan.
Then design and build.
Then test and evaluate.
Then feedback.
Then revise.
And after revise, you return to plan for the next cycle.
Notice how feedback sits in the middle of this loop and drives the revision.
If you were drawing this, it would be a circle, and I would encourage you to look at the accompanying visual so you can see the loop closing on itself.
Next, an important term: the MVP, the minimum viable product.
The source describes it as a minimal safe learning release, and it is explicit that an MVP is not incomplete quality.
Let me stress that.
Minimal refers to the scope, how little it does.
It does not mean sloppy or unfinished in quality.
It is safe, and its purpose is learning: you release it so that you can learn from real use.
What are the benefits of working this way?
Earlier value, because users get something useful sooner.
Visible progress, because stakeholders can see the product growing.
Risk reduction, because problems surface early.
And adaptation, because the team can change direction based on what it learns.
But there are challenges as well.
Integration, because pieces built at different times must fit together.
Architecture erosion, where the original structure gradually degrades.
Technical debt, where shortcuts accumulate and must be paid for later.
Scope creep, where the work keeps expanding.
Feedback overload, where there is too much input to act on sensibly.
And inconsistent stakeholders, where different people give conflicting guidance.
How do we manage these challenges?
The source gives us a list of responses.
Modular design, so that pieces can be added and changed without breaking everything.
A shared Definition of Done, so that everyone agrees what finished means.
Continuous integration and regression testing, so that new work does not break old work.
Product goals, to keep direction clear.
Backlog refinement, to keep the list of work organised and prioritised.
And risk-based release decisions, meaning you decide what to release by weighing the risks.
Finally, let us consider changing requirements, which is a reality in nearly every project.
The source gives an ordered approach.
First, record the new need.
Second, clarify its value and its acceptance criteria.
Third, assess its impact and its dependencies.
Fourth, reorder the backlog together with the Product Owner.
Fifth, protect the current sprint goal.
Sixth, communicate the trade-offs.
And seventh, validate the delivered increments.
One qualification must be remembered.
A change that is legally or operationally urgent may require replanning.
And whatever happens, do not hide new work.
If something new has to be done, it must be made visible, so that the team and stakeholders can see the true picture.
